analysis.one_liner: Blocks the health department from regulating how tobacco is sold, used, or advertised.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 23 cosponsors that would have shielded tobacco from federal health regulation died in a House subcommittee and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forbidden the Secretary of Health and Human Services from regulating the sale or use of tobacco under federal food and drug law, and from taking any new steps under the federal cigarette labeling and advertising laws. It also would have automatically repealed any HHS tobacco regulation that took effect before the bill passed. In plain terms, it would have taken tobacco off the table for the federal health regulator at the very moment the agency was moving to restrict cigarette sales to minors. It never got out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Cigarette and smokeless tobacco manufacturers, whose sales and marketing would remain free of HHS oversight, and tobacco growers and dealers whose crop's market would be protected from regulatory pressure. Supporters argued it also protected tobacco-farming communities from an agency they viewed as overstepping its legal authority.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from regulating the sale or use of tobacco or tobacco products under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

Bars any new HHS action under the Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act or the Comprehensive Smokeless Tobacco Health Education Act of 1986 beyond what was authorized before the bill's passage, freezing the existing rules in place.
Automatically repeals any HHS regulation on the sale or use of tobacco that takes effect before the bill is enacted, clearing away rules then in motion.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers and especially young people, who would go without federal protections on youth access to cigarettes and tobacco marketing; the broader public bears the health costs of smoking left unregulated by the nation's health agency.

drawbacks.text: The bill would repeal, retroactively, any HHS tobacco regulation taking effect before enactment, so protections already in motion would be undone rather than merely prevented.
The bill declares that the Secretary never had authority to regulate tobacco, a legal position that forecloses future administrations from acting on youth smoking through the health agency.

Tobacco-state members and growers had a genuine economic stake: the bill's supporters represented districts where tobacco farming and manufacturing were major employers, and a blunt regulatory ban threatened those livelihoods.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tobacco industry and grower communities, the bill offered real protection from an agency they saw as exceeding its authority. But the trade-off for everyone else was severe: it would have permanently locked the nation's health regulator out of the product that is the leading preventable cause of death, just as federal youth-smoking rules were being developed. The costs fell on people who were not part of the bargain.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and sent to its health subcommittee, sat there, and the 104th Congress ended with no vote ever taken.

narrative.text: Rep. Lewis F. Payne Jr. of Virginia introduced the bill on September 7, 1995, joined by 23 cosponsors, 12 Republicans and 11 Democrats, largely from tobacco-producing states.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced.
On September 18, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it remained with no further action.
The 104th Congress ended January 3, 1997, with the bill never reported out of committee and never brought to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public came out ahead: a law that would have permanently blocked federal health regulation of tobacco died quietly in committee. Within a year, the FDA instead issued its own rules restricting cigarette sales to minors, a path this bill was written to foreclose.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public health; the tobacco shield never passed

for.name: Rep. Lewis F. Payne Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill prohibiting HHS from regulating tobacco and gave introductory remarks.

for.name: 23 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (12 Republicans, 11 Democrats), mostly from tobacco-producing states
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members from North Carolina, Kentucky, and Virginia such as Boucher, Hefner, Bunning, Rose, and Clement.

against.name: Rep. Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee of referral and never advanced the bill to a markup or the House floor; it stayed in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan and regional rather than partisan: a Democratic lead sponsor from Virginia with 12 Republican and 11 Democratic cosponsors, concentrated in tobacco states; no chamber vote ever occurred, so opposition lines were never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have kept the industry's products permanently outside HHS regulation of sale, use, and marketing, blocking restrictions on youth access and advertising. Its gain came at the direct expense of public health protections.

Blocking federal regulation shielded demand for the leaf crop in tobacco-producing districts, which is why the cosponsor list clustered there. Their gain depended on keeping a product the health agency wanted to restrict freely sold.
